candidate.answerReason: The intersection is the octahedron whose vertices are the six cube-face centers. It consists of two square pyramids, each with base area 1/2 and height 1/2, giving total volume 1/6.

methods.label: Find the intersection and split it into pyramids
methods.explanation:
First locate the two tetrahedra. Distances between cube vertices are \(1\), \(\sqrt2\), or \(\sqrt3\). A tetrahedron edge cannot have length \(1\), because the ends of a cube edge have no third cube vertex at distance \(1\) from both. It cannot have length \(\sqrt3\), because each cube vertex has only one vertex that far away. Thus every tetrahedron edge is a face diagonal. Choosing one vertex then forces its three partners to be the three vertices across the incident faces.

Label the bottom square \(ABCD\) cyclically, and label the vertices directly above them \(E,F,G,H\). The two tetrahedra are therefore
\[
T=ACFH,\qquad U=BDEG.
\]
To find their intersection, examine how a face of \(U\) cuts \(T\). The midpoints of \(AC,AF,AH\) are the centers of three cube faces. They also lie on \(BD,BE,DE\), respectively, because the diagonals of each square bisect each other. Hence the face plane \(BDE\) cuts off the corner at \(A\) along the triangle joining these three midpoints. This triangle is parallel to the opposite face \(CFH\), by the triangle midsegment theorem.

The other three faces of \(U\) make the corresponding midpoint cuts at \(C,F,H\). These are exactly the four face restrictions for membership in \(U\). On each original face of \(T\), the cuts leave its medial triangle. Together with the four new cut faces, they enclose an octahedron whose six vertices are the edge midpoints of \(T\), namely the six cube-face centers.

The centers of the four vertical cube faces form a horizontal square. Its diagonals are perpendicular and each has length \(1\), so its area is
\[
B=\frac{1\cdot1}{2}=\frac12.
\]
The top and bottom face centers are the two apices, each at height \(1/2\) from this square. The two pyramids have disjoint interiors and fill the octahedron. Its volume is
\[
2\left(\frac13\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12\right)
=\boxed{\frac16},
\]
which is choice D.
methods.levelReason: The proof uses cube geometry, face diagonals, triangle midsegments, square area, and the pyramid volume formula. No spatial vectors or trigonometry are needed.

methods.label: Subtract the four tetrahedral tips
methods.explanation:
Label a bottom face of the unit cube \(ABCD\) cyclically and the vertices above them \(E,F,G,H\). The only regular tetrahedra are \(T=ACFH\) and \(U=BDEG\). To justify this, their common edge length must be a face-diagonal length: cube edges cannot form an equilateral triangle, and each vertex has only one body-diagonally opposite vertex. From any chosen vertex, the three face-diagonally opposite vertices then force the tetrahedron.

Compute the volume of \(T\) by subtracting from the cube. Its four face planes cut off the cube corners at \(B,D,E,G\). Each removed corner tetrahedron has three mutually perpendicular edges of length \(1\), so it has a right-triangle base of area \(1/2\) and height \(1\). These four corner pieces and \(T\) fill the cube with disjoint interiors. Therefore
\[
V(T)=1-4\left(\frac13\cdot\frac12\cdot1\right)
=\frac13.
\]
Now consider the face \(BDE\) of \(U\). It passes through the midpoints of \(AC,AF,AH\): each midpoint is the center of a square cube face and lies on that face's other diagonal. Thus this face cuts a tip from \(T\) at \(A\). The cutting triangle is parallel to \(CFH\), so the tip is a copy of \(T\) with every length halved.

The other three faces of \(U\) cut matching tips from \(C,F,H\). Their interiors are disjoint; the cuts meet at edge midpoints. These four cuts impose all four face conditions of \(U\), so removing the tips leaves exactly \(T\cap U\).

Halving all lengths quarters a base area and halves the height, so each tip has \(1/8\) the volume of \(T\). Consequently,
\[
V(T\cap U)
=\frac13\left(1-4\cdot\frac18\right)
=\boxed{\frac16},
\]
which is choice D.
